title: Best Trucking Software in 2026: ELD, TMS, Fuel Cards and More
summary: The best trucking software by category: TMS, ELD, fuel cards, factoring, load boards, maintenance and safety. What each vendor does well and what to watch for.
body_markdown:
A trucking company in 2026 runs on six or seven kinds of software: an ELD, a TMS, fuel cards, factoring, load boards, maintenance and safety tools. They do not matter equally. The TMS is the one that decides how the business actually runs.


Every load lives in the TMS from tender to invoice. It sets how fast a dispatcher can book freight, how quickly a delivered load turns into an invoice, whether drivers are paid correctly, and how many people the back office needs. The ELD, fuel card, factoring company and load boards all either feed it or read from it. Pick the wrong one and every other tool becomes a source of retyping. Pick the right one and the rest of the stack starts working together.


Below are the vendors carriers shortlist in each category, starting with the TMS, with what each does well and what to watch for. It is written for asset-based carriers running roughly 10 to 500 trucks. Hemut makes one of the TMS platforms listed, so it gets a Watch for line like everyone else.


## Key takeaways


- **The TMS is the most consequential choice.** It runs dispatch, billing and driver pay, and it decides whether your other tools save time or create work.
- **The ELD is the only piece required by law,** but it is a data source. Its value depends on what your TMS does with it.
- **Integrations matter more than feature lists.** Two good tools that do not share data means someone retyping it every day.
- **Legacy platforms still work,** but many were designed before email, EDI and live GPS were the normal way freight moved.


## 1. Transportation management system (TMS)


The TMS holds orders, stops, driver and truck assignments, settlements, billing and usually accounting. It is the one screen dispatch, billing and payroll all share.


### McLeod Software (LoadMaster)


**Good at:** depth. McLeod has been building carrier software since 1985 and LoadMaster is one of the most widely installed TMS platforms in trucking.


**Watch for:** that age shows. Ask for a realistic go-live date, since rollouts of established enterprise platforms often take months. The interface reflects an older generation of software, and much of the automation carriers now expect comes from add-ons or third parties.


### Trimble TMW.Suite


**Good at:** planning and optimization for large enterprise fleets.


**Watch for:** it is built for fleets with in-house IT. Smaller carriers often find it more system than they need.


### Hemut Command


**Good at:** automation. It reads rate confirmations and EDI tenders into loads, makes routine check calls with voice agents, and builds driver settlements from the load record. It also covers fuel and IFTA, factoring paperwork and maintenance records, which most carriers buy separately.


**Watch for:** it is newer than the legacy platforms, so it has fewer years of installs behind it. It is built for asset-based carriers, so pure freight brokerages are not the fit.


### Axon Software


**Good at:** dispatch and accounting tightly linked in one package.


**Watch for:** load entry and driver follow-up are still mostly manual.


### Tailwind TMS


**Good at:** quick setup for small carriers.


**Watch for:** growing fleets can outgrow it as settlements, accounting and integrations get more complex.


### Alvys


**Good at:** a modern cloud interface.


**Watch for:** ask for references at your fleet size and check how much of the back office it covers.


**What to check in any TMS:** how a load gets in (typed, read from email, or EDI), whether driver pay is calculated from the load, whether it reads live position from your ELD, and the go-live timeline for a fleet your size.


## 2. ELD and telematics


FMCSA's ELD rule took effect on December 18, 2017, and since December 16, 2019 every carrier covered by the rule must use a device that is self-certified and registered with FMCSA. Most ELDs now double as GPS tracking, engine data and dash cameras.


### Samsara


**Good at:** polished hardware, AI dash cams and a large integration marketplace.


**Watch for:** it is a telematics platform, not a TMS. Loads, pay and billing still need a separate system.


### Motive (formerly KeepTruckin)


**Good at:** an easy driver app with ELD, dash cams and fleet cards together.


**Watch for:** same as Samsara: strong on the truck, not on the load.


### Geotab


**Good at:** deep engine data and an open platform.


**Watch for:** it is sold through resellers, so your support experience depends on which one you buy from.


### Omnitracs


**Good at:** a long history with large enterprise fleets.


**Watch for:** it is now part of Solera, which is bringing Omnitracs, SmartDrive and Spireon together under Solera Fleet Solutions. Ask what that means for your hardware.


### Trimble Mobility (formerly PeopleNet)


**Good at:** in-cab hardware many large fleets already own.


**Watch for:** it changed hands in February 2025 when Platform Science bought it. Ask about the product roadmap.


Whichever you run, the useful question is what happens to its data. A TMS that reads position directly (Hemut, for example, works with Samsara, Motive, Geotab and Omnitracs) can turn it into ETAs and arrival times on each load instead of a dispatcher calling the driver.


## 3. Fuel cards and IFTA


Fuel is usually a carrier's biggest cost after drivers. A fuel card gives network discounts, limits what drivers can buy and produces the gallon records you need for IFTA, which is due quarterly by the last day of the month after each quarter.


- **EFS (WEX):** large truck stop network. *Watch for:* card data sits in the EFS portal unless your TMS imports it.
- **Comdata (Corpay):** fuel cards plus Comchek codes for lumpers and other cash needs. *Watch for:* some stops accept only one of the two big networks, so check your lanes.
- **AtoB:** a newer card with a modern app. *Watch for:* confirm acceptance and discounts on the stops your drivers actually use.


The quarter-end IFTA spreadsheet is avoidable. Some TMS platforms now import fuel transactions and build the return from your own miles and gallons; Hemut does this with EFS data.


## 4. Factoring


Many carriers sell their invoices to get paid in a day or two instead of waiting 30 to 60 days. **RTS Financial** , **Triumph** and **OTR Solutions** are three of the best-known factors.


*Watch for:* recourse terms, per-invoice fees, and how invoices and proof of delivery reach the factor. If someone in your office is scanning paperwork and emailing it, ask whether your TMS can assemble and send the packet when the load delivers.


## 5. Load boards


Even carriers with contract freight use load boards to fill gaps and find backhauls. **DAT** and **Truckstop** are the two largest.


*Watch for:* on their own, load boards are a second screen. The useful question is how fast a posting becomes a booked load in your TMS without retyping it.


## 6. Maintenance


Preventive maintenance keeps trucks out of the shop and out of roadside out-of-service orders.


- **Fleetio:** a capable standalone maintenance app. *Watch for:* it is one more system to keep in sync with your truck list.
- **TMT Fleet Maintenance (Trimble):** built for big shops. *Watch for:* heavy for fleets without a full-time shop manager.
- **Whip Around:** simple driver inspections. *Watch for:* inspections only, not full maintenance history.


## 7. Safety and compliance


Your safety record is public. Shippers and brokers check your authority, insurance and inspection history before they tender freight. Dash cams from your ELD vendor or specialists such as **Lytx** help with coaching and claims.


It is worth looking up your own USDOT number the way a broker would. Our free[carrier lookup](https://hemut.com/carrier-lookup) shows authority, insurance, out-of-service orders and inspection results in one place.

## How to choose


1. **Keep your ELD.** Swapping hardware is expensive and rarely necessary. Make sure the TMS reads from it.
2. **Spend the most time on the TMS,** judged by how loads get in and how much of the back office it covers.
3. **Count the logins.** Every separate tool is a place where data gets retyped and something gets missed.
4. **Ask for a live handoff demo.** Have each vendor show a rate confirmation becoming a load, the load getting a live ETA, and the delivered load becoming an invoice and a driver settlement.


## FAQ


### What software is legally required for a trucking company?


For most interstate carriers, only an FMCSA-registered ELD. Some short-haul and older-vehicle exemptions apply. Everything else is a business choice.


### Can one product cover everything?


Not the ELD hardware, which stays with your telematics vendor. Beyond that, newer TMS platforms increasingly fold in fuel, IFTA, factoring paperwork and maintenance, which cuts the number of systems to keep in sync.


### Is McLeod still a good choice?


For very large fleets with in-house IT and years of customization already in place, it can be. Carriers starting fresh or outgrowing spreadsheets usually want something faster to set up and more automated.


### How long does it take to switch a TMS?


It depends on fleet size, integrations and how much history you bring over. Ask each vendor for the go-live timeline of a customer your size, and talk to that customer.
